name: Boccaccio on the plague and the price of nursing
author: Giovanni Boccaccio
work: Decameron, Introduction to the First Day
text: brother forsook brother, uncle nephew and sister brother and oftentimes wife husband; nay (what is yet more extraordinary and well nigh incredible) fathers and mothers refused to visit or tend their very children, as they had not been theirs. By reason whereof there remained unto those (and the number of them, both males and females, was incalculable) who fell sick, none other succour than that which they owed either to the charity of friends (and of these there were few) or the greed of servants, who tended them, allured by high and extravagant wage
witness: Boccaccio wrote the frame of the Decameron c.1349-51 in Florence, where his father probably died of the plague. It is a literary set piece modelled partly on Thucydides and Paul the Deacon, so the breakdown of family duty is heightened for effect, but the detail that nursing now cost "high and extravagant wage" is exactly the labour-market shock that wage series show.

sources.cite: Decameron, Introduction to the First Day

name: Boccaccio on Florence's dead and the abandoned fields
author: Giovanni Boccaccio
work: Decameron, Introduction to the First Day
text: the oxen, the asses, the sheep, the goats, the swine, the fowls, nay, the very dogs, so faithful to mankind, being driven forth of their own houses, went straying at their pleasure about the fields, where the very corn was abandoned, without being cut, much less gathered in; and many, well nigh like reasonable creatures, after grazing all day, returned at night, glutted, to their houses, without the constraint of any herdsman. ... it is believed for certain that upward of an hundred thousand human beings perished within the walls of the city of Florence, which, peradventure, before the advent of that death-dealing calamity, had not been accounted to hold so many?
witness: The figure of 100,000 dead is a rhetorical number: Florence probably held 90,000 to 120,000 people before 1348 and lost around half. The image of livestock wandering unherded over unharvested fields is a topos, but it matches manorial evidence that labour, not land, was suddenly scarce.

sources.cite: Decameron, Introduction to the First Day

name: Froissart on English serfdom and the rebels' demand for wages
author: Jean Froissart
work: Chronicles, II, on the rising of 1381 (Berners translation)
text: There was an usage in England, and yet is in divers countries, that the noblemen hath great franchise over the commons and keepeth them in servage ... These unhappy people of these said countries began to stir, because they said they were kept in great servage ... the which they said they would no longer suffer, for they would be all one, and if they laboured or did anything for their lords, they would have wages therefor as well as other.
witness: Froissart, a courtly chronicler from Hainault writing for noble patrons in the 1390s, was not in England in 1381 and despised the rebels. That makes his summary of their grievance, that bondmen wanted to be paid wages like everyone else, the more telling. Berners's Tudor English translation (1520s) is followed by the Harvard Classics text.

sources.cite: Chronicles, II, on the rising of 1381 (Berners translation)

name: John Ball's sermon as Froissart reports it
author: Jean Froissart
work: Chronicles, II, on the rising of 1381 (Berners translation)
text: What have we deserved, or why should we be kept thus in servage? We be all come from one father and one mother, Adam and Eve: whereby can they say or shew that they be greater lords than we be, saving by that they cause us to win and labour for that they dispend?
witness: These are Froissart's words put into the mouth of the radical priest John Ball, not a transcript; the chronicler calls him a "foolish priest". The appeal to common descent from Adam and Eve is attested in English sources too (the "When Adam delved" couplet), so the substance is probably genuine even if the speech is composed.

sources.cite: Chronicles, II, on the rising of 1381 (Berners translation)

name: A Ciompi leader's speech, as Machiavelli wrote it
author: Niccolò Machiavelli
text: Be not deceived about that antiquity of blood by which they exalt themselves above us; for all men having had one common origin, are all equally ancient, and nature has made us all after one fashion. Strip us naked, and we shall all be found alike. Dress us in their clothing, and they in ours, we shall appear noble, they ignoble--for poverty and riches make all the difference.
witness: Machiavelli wrote this speech some 145 years after the event, in the classical manner of invented orations; it voices his own view of power more than any wool carder's. It shows how the revolt was remembered in Medici Florence, not what was said. The translator of this 1901 edition is unnamed.

name: Thomas More: sheep that devour men
author: Thomas More
text: The increase of pasture,’ said I, ‘by which your sheep, which are naturally mild, and easily kept in order, may be said now to devour men and unpeople, not only villages, but towns; for wherever it is found that the sheep of any soil yield a softer and richer wool than ordinary, there the nobility and gentry, and even those holy men, the abbots! not contented with the old rents which their farms yielded, nor thinking it enough that they, living at their ease, do no good to the public, resolve to do it hurt instead of good. They stop the course of agriculture, destroying houses and towns, reserving only the churches, and enclose grounds that they may lodge their sheep in them.
witness: Spoken by More's fictional traveller Hythloday in a satire written by a London lawyer and royal servant. Enclosure was real but more gradual than the image suggests; Tudor commissions of 1517 found depopulation concentrated in the Midlands. Burnet's 1684 translation from the Latin.

name: Luther's 86th thesis: why does the pope not pay?
author: Martin Luther
text: Why does not the pope, whose wealth is to-day greater than the riches of the richest, build just this one church of St. Peter with his own money, rather than with the money of poor believers?
witness: Luther frames this as one of the "shrewd questions of the laity", a Latin academic disputation thesis of October 1517, not a popular pamphlet; it went viral only when printers reissued the theses in Nuremberg, Leipzig and Basel. English translation in the 1915 Philadelphia edition of Luther's Works.

name: Bacon on printing, gunpowder and the compass
author: Francis Bacon
text: Again, we should notice the force, effect, and consequences of inventions, which are nowhere more conspicuous than in those three which were unknown to the ancients; namely, printing, gunpowder, and the compass. For these three have changed the appearance and state of the whole world: first in literature, then in warfare, and lastly in navigation; and innumerable changes have been thence derived, so that no empire, sect, or star, appears to have exercised a greater power and influence on human affairs than these mechanical discoveries.
witness: Bacon, Lord Chancellor and promoter of experimental science, wanted to show that the moderns had outdone the ancients. All three inventions came from China, which he did not know; read it as a European self-image at the start of the 17th century. Devey's 1902 edition of the English translation.

name: Hobbes: solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short
author: Thomas Hobbes
text: In such condition, there is no place for Industry; because the fruit thereof is uncertain; and consequently no Culture of the Earth; no Navigation, nor use of the commodities that may be imported by Sea; no commodious Building; no Instruments of moving, and removing such things as require much force; no Knowledge of the face of the Earth; no account of Time; no Arts; no Letters; no Society; and which is worst of all, continuall feare, and danger of violent death; And the life of man, solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short.
witness: Written in Paris exile and published in London in 1651 as the civil wars ended. Hobbes describes a thought experiment, the state of nature, not England; but every item on his list of what war destroys (farming, trade, building, letters) was being lost somewhere in Europe in the 1640s. Spelling of the 1651 first edition.

name: Adam Smith: the two greatest events in the history of mankind
author: Adam Smith
work: Wealth of Nations, Book IV, chapter 7, part 3
text: The discovery of America, and that of a passage to the East Indies by the Cape of Good Hope, are the two greatest and most important events recorded in the history of mankind. ... To the natives, however, both of the East and West Indies, all the commercial benefits which can have resulted from those events have been sunk and lost in the dreadful misfortunes which they have occasioned. These misfortunes, however, seem to have arisen rather from accident than from any thing in the nature of those events themselves. At the particular time when these discoveries were made, the superiority of force happened to be so great on the side of the Europeans, that they were enabled to commit with impunity every sort of injustice in those remote countries.
witness: Smith wrote against the mercantile system and the monopoly companies, so he stresses the gains of free exchange and the injustice of conquest. His explanation of European success as a contingent "superiority of force" anticipates the military-revolution debate.

sources.cite: Wealth of Nations, Book IV, chapter 7, part 3

name: Montaigne: mechanic victories
author: Michel de Montaigne
text: So many cities levelled with the ground, so many nations exterminated, so many millions of people fallen by the edge of the sword, and the richest and most beautiful part of the world turned upside down, for the traffic of pearl and pepper? Mechanic victories! Never did ambition, never did public animosities, engage men against one another in such miserable hostilities
witness: Montaigne, a Bordeaux magistrate who never crossed the Atlantic, drew on Spanish chroniclers such as López de Gómara; the essay is a moral reflection, not reportage. Its point, that the conquest was won by technique ("mechanic victories") and paid for with depopulation, is close to modern accounts. Cotton's 1685 translation, Hazlitt's edition.
